## Discussion

LTR speakers replicated the well-documented leftward bias, and both groups fixated upward well above chance. RTL speakers' leftward proportion sat almost exactly at chance and, on its own, was indistinguishable from no preference at all. The confirmatory test tells a clearer story than that proportion does. Once each arrangement's own baseline pull is accounted for, the two groups differ (b = 1.08, p = .009), and splitting the test by axis puts most of that difference on the horizontal one (b = 1.32 for left/right against b = 0.70 for up/down). The single cleanest comparison is the 9-3 arrangement, where the choice is left against right with no vertical component at all: LTR looked right first on 12.5% of trials, RTL on 48.8%. Arrangement still explains more of the variance than group does, but the group effect is not marginal and it points where reading direction predicts.

### Relation to the literature

LTR's leftward proportion (71.8%) sits inside the 60-93% range reported by Foulsham et al. [-@foulsham2013] and Ossandón et al. [-@ossandon2014], though below the roughly 80% that Ehinger et al. [-@ehinger2026] found for German speakers in the same horizontal arrangement. Composition probably accounts for part of that gap: our LTR group is nine English and two German speakers, not a purely German sample. The counting task may account for another part, since it asked participants to engage with both images rather than glance and move on. Neither would contradict the earlier result.

RTL's proportion (49.0%) fits a "reduced, not reversed" account. Chokron and Imbert [-@chokron1993] and Rashidi-Ranjbar et al. [-@rashidi2014] found weaker or reversed leftward bias in Arabic, Hebrew, and mixed-reading-habit populations doing line bisection; ours lands on chance rather than reversing outright. Afsari et al. [-@afsari2016] showed native RTL readers shift rightward after an RTL priming passage but leftward after an LTR one, while late-acquired RTL readers show no such flexibility. Our participants read a story in their own language but were not primed with the contrast, so a near-chance default is a sensible baseline for priming to move away from in either direction. That the pooled proportion sits at chance while the arrangement-adjusted regression finds a reliable difference suggests the horizontal habit is real but weak enough to be swamped, in a simple proportion, by each arrangement's own pull.

The vertical result is the one the hypotheses did not anticipate. RTL's upward bias (83.4%) is larger than LTR's (72.6%), and reading direction is a horizontal habit; neither the right-hemisphere lateralization account [@corbetta2002] nor the cross-linguistic account predicts a group difference on this axis. The arrangement effects in the regression suggest a possible reason. The three arrangements without an upper-left stimulus (7-1, 8-2 and 12-6) are exactly the three where RTL's slow-latency tail grows, and 12-6 is where its vertical preference becomes near-absolute: RTL fixated the lower stimulus first on 2 of 79 trials, against 13.6% of trials for LTR. That reads as a fallback: when an arrangement offers no upper-left target for the horizontal bias to lock onto, both groups lean harder on the vertical one, and RTL leans hardest because it has less horizontal pull to begin with. The data are consistent with this account without confirming it. The arrangement-by-group interaction that would test it directly does converge, but with 10 RTL subjects spread across twelve cells and no clustered fit computed, it is not a reliable per-arrangement test (see Limitations). If the account is right, the upward bias would be closer to a general property of the attentional system than a culturally modulated one, a distinction the horizontal-axis literature reviewed in the Introduction does not address.

Individual variability sits underneath all of this. Foulsham et al. [-@foulsham2018] report that leftward viewing biases are stable within a person but unrelated to handedness or line-bisection performance, that is, a real trait that does not reduce cleanly to the usual explanations. Our quadrant plot shows the same texture. Five subjects lean rightward and no LTR subject is among them, which lines up with the group means, but the LTR points themselves range from -0.15 to -0.90 on the same axis, and two of them show no vertical preference at all while every RTL subject does. The group means are real, and they sit on top of individual variation that the group-level story does not reach.

### Limitations

The RTL group is smaller than LTR's, ten subjects and 474 trials against eleven and 523, and every RTL confidence interval reflects it. The descriptive left/right proportion is the clearest case: at 49.0% it cannot be told apart from no preference on its own, and only the arrangement-adjusted models recover the group difference. Clustering standard errors by subject, the correct choice given non-independent trials, is what separates the regression's naive p < .001 from its clustered p = .009. The effect survives that correction on both axes, but with 21 subjects the intervals stay wide, and this is the same power problem Ehinger et al. [-@ehinger2026] describe for spatial-bias designs generally.

Group membership follows the native language a participant selected and was recruited under, rather than a formal history questionnaire covering age of acquisition or biliteracy, so a lateralization confound from atypical or mixed reading histories cannot be fully ruled out. Reading direction is also confounded with everything else that differs between four languages and their speakers: culture, script, the translated story text, the recruitment pool. A between-subjects design with 21 people cannot separate reading direction from these co-varying factors; it can only describe the group difference, not attribute it.

The arrangement-by-group interaction, which would give each arrangement its own group comparison and test the vertical fallback account directly, converges but is not trustworthy at this sample size: 10 RTL subjects across twelve cells, one of them nearly unanimous (2 of 79 trials went to the lower stimulus), and no clustered version of the model fitted. The hour-by-hour and arrangement-by-arrangement differences described above therefore remain descriptive.

The counting task required participants to engage with both images rather than only the one fixated first, which is a deliberate departure from pure free viewing. First-fixation latency stayed fast, with medians between 248 and 285 ms in every arrangement, which argues against much top-down influence on the very first saccade, but it does not rule out a subtler effect of knowing a count would be required. Finally, demographic variables like age and sex are not yet available for this sample.

### Challenges during the project

The clock-face recoding turned out to be necessary, not optional. The raw log's `img_left`/`img_right` labels track each pair's position along the clock diameter, not physical screen sides, so for every non-horizontal arrangement one of "left" and "right" was really "top" or "bottom". This surfaced only once the vertical and diagonal arrangements were analyzed, and the fix, recoding every trial by the clock hour actually fixated, had to happen before any left/right or up/down contrast could be trusted.

Display scaling caused trouble twice, in two different places. Two participants (43, 44) were run before a scaling bug in the experiment script was caught, and it made their online-logged first-fixation values unusable: both showed a leftward or absent first fixation on all 96 combined trials, which offline recomputation from the raw gaze stream showed to be wrong in both cases. That recomputation became the pipeline for every participant once the online log could no longer be trusted uniformly. The same distinction between OpenSesame's 1536 x 864 coordinate space and the 1920 x 1080 display then bit the offline pipeline too, which compared gaze in display pixels against stimulus positions in script coordinates and so placed every area of interest about 77 px too close to the center of the screen. Fixation positions during the trials made the error visible and easy to check, and correcting it left the conclusions intact, but it is a reminder that a coordinate space is worth writing down explicitly rather than inferring.

Recruiting native RTL speakers was harder than recruiting LTR speakers, which is the direct cause of the eleven-to-ten imbalance and, downstream, of the power problem described above. Quality control also caught calibration problems in two participants (61, 107) only after full data collection, when the sessions could no longer be corrected. And running the study in four languages (German, English, Arabic, Persian) meant translating the story text, instructions, and comprehension questions into all four, coordinated across a small team, on top of the core eye-tracking design.

### Outlook

Adding a formal native-language history questionnaire, covering age of acquisition and biliteracy rather than self-reported language selection alone, would narrow the lateralization confound instead of leaving it as a design limitation.

The vertical-fallback account is testable on its own. A follow-up powered specifically for an arrangement (upper-left target present versus absent) by group interaction would confirm or rule it out, rather than relying on the descriptive pattern reported here. It also suggests a concrete revision to Ehinger et al.'s [-@ehinger2026] stimulus-placement recommendation for mixed-language samples: rather than picking one diagonal arrangement that is neutral for a single population, a design could place each group's preferred target so both groups' biases are equally engaged, since the arrangements that produced the largest group divergence here were exactly the ones offering neither group its usual upper-left anchor.

Two things would be worth changing about the pipeline itself. Logging the clock-hour position directly, instead of `img_left`/`img_right`, would remove the recoding step and the ambiguity that could have gone unnoticed if the vertical and diagonal arrangements had not been checked closely. Logging stimulus positions in display pixels, or at least recording the display scale alongside them, would have prevented both scaling problems outright. Running the offline recomputation against a few pilot sessions before full data collection would also have caught the first of them immediately, rather than after two participants' data needed a separate fix.
